# Shared-device playtest notes

This page is a qualitative account of how people played Neon Pairs together and what those sessions suggest for competition design.

The sessions examined local play with the current game. The observations concern attention, learning and handoff.

## Session setting

The working setup was deliberately modest: one browser game, people seated close enough to see the screen and paper notes beside the device. Event sketches were discussed on paper because the game has no participant entry or bracket controller. The browser supplied the actual card play, its ordinary status area and the existing reproduction tools.

Three settings were considered: a laptop on a table, a tablet passed between adjacent seats and a phone held by the current player. These are contrasting situations, not a representative sample of device usage. Their value was in making different problems observable. A laptop makes spectating easy; a held phone makes physical transfer and changing viewing angles much more prominent.

The discussion concentrated on what people did without prompting. Could someone enter the board, distinguish a face, recover after a miss and understand that their board was complete? Could a person who had looked away rejoin the conversation? Those questions were more productive than asking participants whether a finished competition feature sounded appealing in the abstract.

## Laptop: learning the faces aloud

In the laptop session, Mara began with the pointer and described each revealed face aloud. Her first descriptions used only shape: circle, star, triangle. After encountering similar shapes with different markers in a larger practice board, she started adding direction. The vocabulary changed from “the star near the corner” to “the star with the marker on the right.”

Jon, sitting beside her, remembered locations in row terms instead. He pointed to a horizontal band and then counted columns. They were attending to the same artwork but encoding different information. Neither strategy suggested a problem with the deck; the difference was in how people organized memory.

This observation agrees with the face model in `src/game/board/face-design.ts`: shape and marker direction both contribute to identity, and the game also includes a fill distinction. It also explains why the introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker. A report that two faces “looked the same” can mean that a participant initially remembered only part of the available design.

The useful follow-up question was which feature they had noticed, rather than whether they had memorized the official face name. [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) and [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) provide the source context for interpreting such reports.

## Keyboard: movement looked like hesitation

Leah used Tab to enter the board and then moved with the arrows. An observer initially wrote down several pauses as indecision about the puzzle. On closer discussion, some of those pauses were time spent checking the focus outline and moving to a remembered position. The participant knew which card she wanted before she reached it.

This was a useful correction to the observation method. Card navigation and memory retrieval are separate activities, even when they occur between the same two reveals. Counting only the delay between clicks would have concealed the difference entirely, since this participant was not primarily clicking.

Leah also revisited an already matched card while moving across the board. She treated it as a landmark rather than as a card she intended to play. The current cards remain focusable in that state. That behavior made sense in the session, but an observer looking only at focus position might have misclassified it as a failed selection.

The input trace records navigation behavior. The repository README records accessibility-tree checks; screen-reader testing has not been performed. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md), [focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [screen reader notes](../interface/screen-reader-notes.md) distinguish those subjects.

## Tablet: the handoff was an activity of its own

In the tablet session, moving the device between people interrupted the group's visual reference. The outgoing player tilted it toward the next person, while another participant tried to read the result from an angle. The result was still present, but not everyone saw it at the same time.

The next player first adjusted the tablet on the table, then looked for the board. That sequence would have been easy to describe as slow play if the observer had measured from physical handoff. It was mostly positioning the device. The observation helped separate the social transition from actual interaction with the game.

People also used the visible completed board as a conversation piece. They pointed at remembered mistakes and explained how they finally located a pair. The exposed cards carried a short history of the attempt that a bare result number would not capture. In a group setting, that retrospective conversation was part of the appeal.

The presentation of a competition handoff remained undecided. The prototype used ordinary play and a paper event sketch. It showed what people looked at and discussed. [Competition overview](competition-overview.md) explains the intended social context.

## Phone: scrolling and tapping had different purposes

On the phone, Niko sometimes touched the board to move its visible area rather than to reveal a card. His comments made that intention clear: he was searching for a remembered row near the edge. A raw touch trace would have contained contact with several cards, but contact alone would not have described the intended action.

The research note therefore distinguishes an attempted tap, a completed activation and a scroll gesture. These are useful observational categories, not additional game states. A participant saying “I touched that one” can refer to any of them, and the distinction can explain an apparent missing move.

The observer's view was narrower on the phone too. People beside the player often saw the device's back or an oblique angle, so they talked more about the eventual result than about individual reveals. That was a different social experience from the laptop, even though the underlying card actions were unchanged. [Pointer and touch](../interface/pointer-and-touch.md) and [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md) cover the relevant existing behavior.

## The mismatch pause helped memory and confused tapping

Several exchanges centered on a miss. One participant used the visible interval to repeat both face descriptions aloud. Another tapped quickly again and interpreted the lack of a new reveal as a lost input. The two reactions came from different expectations about whether the turn had finished.

It was useful in the discussion to replay the participant's explanation in ordinary language: “I was still looking at those two” versus “I thought I could choose the next one.” Both describe a reading of the same moment. Neither requires a different deck or a new scoring mechanism to explain it.

## Spectators remembered more than the current player expected

People who watched closely often remembered a location that the player had forgotten. Sometimes that produced a laugh; sometimes it produced an unsolicited hint. When the device moved out of view, conversation changed from specific positions to general encouragement. The physical setting strongly influenced how much information was shared.

This is relevant to the feel of local competition. The current application has no way to know who watched the screen or who spoke during a turn. No screen arrangement can make that social history part of the board code. The notes identify a design tension.

A future research session could explore how different groups feel about spectating, but that is a research question rather than a committed feature. The existing observations support only the narrower conclusion that sharing a device also shares attention in ways that vary with posture, distance and familiarity.

## Evidence retained from the discussion

These sessions identified misunderstandings during local play. Shape-only memory, keyboard travel, device adjustment and the visible mismatch interval each explain a different kind of report. The observations are useful starting points for further sessions.

A board code can anchor an arrangement, a snapshot can anchor progress and a replay can anchor actions. The observer's account adds the human context those artifacts omit. [Competition deals](competition-deals.md), [browser test guide](../quality/browser-test-guide.md) and [acceptance](../quality/acceptance.md) explain the technical evidence.

# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the [reproducibility formats](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

## Components

- A07 - `Game.tsx` composes status, the board, game controls and reproduction controls. Keep board navigation in `src/game/board`, controls in `src/game/controls` and session behavior in `src/game/session`. Keep each component's props and styles beside it.

- A08 - A card mounts its face SVG only while revealed or matched. Hidden card identity stays out of DOM attributes, accessible names and diagnostic globals. Tests can know a deck from its documented board code. The app gives them no solver endpoint.

- A09 - Use native browser input and the shared card activation function. Keep focus position in the board component. Focus movement changes presentation, never the deck or move count. [Input](../interface/input.md) defines the keys and focus rules.

## Evidence

- A10 - Keep focused tests beside their behavior. Complete browser journeys live at the application test level. Check generation against independent literal vectors. Check game transitions against stated rules. Test built HTML from disk as well as served storage behavior.

- A11 - Keep development fixtures and diagnostic helpers out of the shipped game. Tests can use the documented board code, snapshot and replay formats. The shipped game exposes only its documented controls.

## Changes

- A12 - Add a new rule at its game behavior, then update its component, tests and specification. Add shared support only when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. Don't add a global store, event bus, router or generic utility folder.

The [game specification](../README.md) defines the behavior this structure implements.

# Module layout policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs places behavior in the source tree and how to extend that structure without obscuring the game rules.

The current tree is small enough to read directly. It has no application framework around the game, no route hierarchy and no general service container. `src/main.tsx` mounts `Game`; the application then divides into rule functions, a session adapter and components for the board, controls and status. [Source layout](source-layout.md) is the file inventory. This page explains the choices behind it.

## Follow behavior before file type

The board directory contains `Board.tsx`, `Card.tsx`, `Face.tsx`, navigation helpers, card descriptions, face design, styles and focused tests. Its contents answer a coherent set of questions: how a position is presented, how focus moves and how a face becomes visible. A separate top-level directory for every hook, type or stylesheet would make those questions harder to answer.

The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.

This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.

## The dependency direction

The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.

The session layer points inward. `session.ts` calls `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `createGame` and `isWon`, then adds session feedback, import pause state and best-score decisions. `use-game.ts` provides callable actions to components. The UI receives values and actions; it does not become the only place where a legal turn can be computed.

There are intentional lateral imports. `storage.ts` uses `GRID_SIZES` and `MOVES_MAX` to validate preferences against actual game limits. `card-state.ts` uses `faceDesign` to describe a visible face. These relationships connect meanings that genuinely belong together. They do not form a general helpers layer with unrelated operations.

A useful way to inspect an unfamiliar change is to start at its public behavior and follow direct imports toward the core. A card click leads through the controller to `activateSession` and `activateCard`. A loaded snapshot leads through `decodeSnapshot`, `readMatched` and `readSelection`. The direction remains visible because there are no barrel files hiding which definition is used.

## State is divided by meaning

`GameState` extends the board description with matched positions, the current selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and a start flag. It does not store a focus position or a form draft. The board description includes its code, size, seed and deck. `generateBoard` freezes the description and deck at runtime, while the TypeScript interfaces expose readonly fields.

`Session` wraps that game with `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. A generation identifies a replacement deal. It is not a move count and does not belong in a snapshot. Feedback belongs here because turn results and imports need session-level presentation, while replay needs only the final game state.

The board hook owns its remembered focused index. `Reproduction` owns the textarea draft. `BoardCodeForm` uses an uncontrolled input initialized from the current code, with its generation key causing a fresh input on replacement. These values have useful local lifetimes. Moving them into `GameState` would make serialization and rule transitions depend on presentation details.

## Splitting a file

Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

The current snapshot split is instructive. `snapshot.ts` owns the outer format, byte bound, numeric fields, serialization and consistency checks. `snapshot-selection.ts` owns the nested selection and matched-position interpretation. Both operate on the same domain, but their validation tasks are distinct enough to read independently. `saved-format.ts` holds the small operations actually shared by snapshot, replay and preferences.

The clock split follows a different seam. `browser-clock.ts` performs arithmetic on supplied observations. `use-session-clock.ts` owns observation, scheduling, visibility and cleanup. Splitting those by arbitrary line count would lose the reason for the boundary. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows the interaction in detail.

A file can stay short while still carrying several unrelated concerns. Conversely, a dense type and a straightforward exhaustive branch may reasonably live together. The existing architecture asks for splitting by behavior, so a review considers what a reader would need to understand together before considering the final line count.

## Imports expose the owner

The source uses static ESM imports with `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes. Types are imported with `import type` or an inline `type` marker. `use-game.ts` imports the snapshot decoder directly from `../snapshot.ts`; it does not import an application-wide registry. `Controls.tsx` imports `GRID_SIZES` from `../deck.ts`, where supported sizes are defined.

That directness matters when a symbol changes. `SelectionKind` is the owner of the selection discriminants; both rules and validators use it. `MISMATCH_MS` is defined beside turn resolution and imported where an interval bound is needed. A second constant with the same current number would hide a semantic disagreement until a later change.

The source convention tests also inspect exported values. They look for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. [Source audit notes](source-audit-notes.md) describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. [CSS organization](css-organization.md) traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior. Neither change calls for a new game-state field.

A correction to imported mismatch validity belongs in `snapshot-selection.ts`; a change to the loading pause belongs in `session.ts` or `use-game.ts`. They may share a user journey, but they answer different questions: whether the submitted data describes a valid game and how the browser enters that valid game.

A turn-count defect belongs in `activateCard`. The displayed statistic and exported snapshot already consume its result. Fixing the number in `GameStatus` would leave replay, completion and storage observing the old value. These examples are consequences of the existing structure, not extra parallel implementations.

For review, [Code review guide](code-review-guide.md) starts from the behavior changed and follows these seams. For the larger rationale, [Architecture](architecture.md) remains the specification of the core, browser session and component boundaries.

# Session module

This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences.

The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides a controller for components; the clock and storage hooks perform effects. Keeping those roles distinct makes it possible to explain a click as a sequence of ordinary data decisions followed by rendering and persistence.

## The Session value

`Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves.

These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state.

The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model.

## Initialization

`initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences.

The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Active progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot.

`browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called.

## The current ref and React state

`useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`.

This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game.

The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) follows the component consequences.

## Card activation

The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match.

`activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet.

For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn.

A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus.

## Why feedback has an event counter

Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.

A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice.

`loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message.

## Replacing a game

`replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices.

If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation.

A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves.

The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.

## Controller actions

| Controller action | Validation or preparation | Session effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `newGame(size?)` | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game |
| `restart()` | Recreate the current code, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game of that deal |
| `loadBoard(code)` | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice |
| `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice |
| `exportSnapshot()` | Synchronize active clock | Encode latest game and return text |
| `activate(index)` | Synchronize active clock | Apply session activation |
| `resume()` | Reset observation baseline | Clear pause and load feedback |

The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically.

The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact.

## Logical ticks

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too.

A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer.

The hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details scheduling, visibility and fractional steps.

## Preferences and effects

`Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`.

`rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect.

`useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails.

The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method.

## Focus is a neighboring concern

The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session.

## Evidence and investigation

`session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture.

`storage.test.ts` supplies stores that work and stores whose methods throw. Browser environment tests additionally make acquisition of localStorage fail. This separates the browser integration failure from validation and operation failures in the narrow store interface.

For an incorrect result, inspecting `activateCard` establishes the game transition first. If the game is right but the notice, celebration or preference is wrong, `activateSession` and `replaceGame` are the next places to inspect. If the data is right but an interaction sees old values, the controller's synchronization and commit path become relevant. The directory's separation makes those questions answerable without debugging the entire component tree at once.

# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. [Clock design](clock-design.md) discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md) covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows those cases in detail, and [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runners.

# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

## One action path for activation

`Card` renders a native button and invokes its supplied activation callback from `onClick`. Native keyboard activation and ordinary pointer activation therefore reach the same controller action. The keydown handler delegates navigation; it does not implement another matching algorithm.

The controller synchronizes active time and calls `activateSession`, which calls `activateCard`. Components receive the resulting state and render it. A class such as `matched` is an outcome of the data, not the authoritative record of a matched pair. Reading CSS classes back into the core would reverse that relationship.

Matched buttons use `aria-disabled`, keeping them in the board's focus model. The rule function still rejects activating matched positions. During a mismatch, the session does not mark every other button disabled; the core rejects new activations while that selection is pending. Semantic presentation and transition legality are both visible, with legality centralized in the rules.

## Latest values without another store

`useGame` keeps React state for rendering and a ref for immediate event-time access. `commit` updates the ref before setting React state. A clock synchronization can therefore commit a new game, and the immediately following activation can consume that new game in the same task.

The board has a similar but narrower pattern for callback identity. `Game` supplies a new activation function as it renders. `Board` stores that function in `latestActivate`, updates the ref in a layout effect and passes a stable `useCallback` wrapper to cards. Memoized cards see a stable function prop while it calls the latest controller closure.

These refs do not bypass the rules. They keep the correct data/action visible across render scheduling. The data transition still returns a new immutable description, and React still receives the committed session. [Session module](session-module.md) explains why the current ref matters for export and activation boundaries.

## Render cost on a large board

A 16 by 16 board has 256 cards. Active time can update on the 40ms observation cadence, but most ticks do not change any card's appearance. `advanceGame` retains the deck and matched array and, outside a mismatch change, retains the selection object. `Board` memoizes face-up and matched sets from those references.

`Card` is wrapped in `memo`. Its props are primitive presentation values and stable callbacks. On an elapsed-only update, face, matched, tabIndex, size and handlers stay equal, so the cards do not all need to rerender. The parent can still update the statistic.

A pending mismatch changes selection as its remainder decreases, so the face-up set can be recomputed. The resulting card props can nevertheless remain equal until the selection actually closes. This distinction explains why immutable reference stability is useful even though the board's parent renders more often than its cards.

Memoization is not a substitute for correct state ownership. Mutating the matched array in place could keep its reference stable while changing its meaning, causing derived sets to miss an update. The transition code returns a new matched array when a pair is found, matching the assumptions of the board's memoization.

## Concealed identity is a prop boundary

`Board` knows the immutable deck, but it passes `face={null}` for every position outside the derived face-up set. `Card` then renders only a decorative back. It does not mount `Face` and hide it with CSS. Its accessible description omits face design when the supplied face is null.

When revealed or matched, a card gets the face number and renders inline SVG. `Face` marks the SVG as decorative, while the button's label describes the visible design. The board can therefore hold authoritative identity without exposing concealed identity through every child element.

This behavior is also why tests use documented board codes rather than a diagnostic global. A test can reconstruct a deal independently and activate matching positions through the public interface. There is no application solver endpoint that a production user or test needs to query.

## Local focus and DOM work

`useBoardFocus` holds a focused index initialized to zero and refs to the viewport and grid. Arrow handling calls `navigationTarget`; a non-null result prevents the browser default and focuses the target button with `preventScroll: true`. Focus events update the remembered index.

`useNearestScroll` listens to the board viewport's scroll events and remembers the reported position. For keyboard focus it restores that position before calling `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. This accounts for Chromium's automatic centering on focus. A click scrolls after activation so the pressed card is not moved under a held pointer before release.

These browser operations belong with the board presentation, not `GameState`. A replay contains positions and logical times, not a scroll offset. A snapshot can load into a differently sized viewport. Keeping focus and scrolling local preserves that independence.

## Replacement and imperative focus

`Game` gives `Board` a ref typed as `BoardFocus`. The board exposes only `focusRemembered()` through `useImperativeHandle`. The parent does not receive the whole grid DOM or a collection of card nodes.

Resume uses that limited operation, then calls the controller's resume action. A replacement instead increments generation and changes the board key, remounting its local focus state. `BoardCodeForm` keys its uncontrolled input by that same generation, so successful loading replaces the old draft with the current code.

A generation is consequently a lifecycle boundary shared by adapters and components. It is not a reason to put DOM state in the session core. The rule functions remain unaware of keyed mounts, refs or focus methods.

## Effects and cleanup

Browser effects pair setup with cleanup: the clock removes its listener and timeout, and nearest scrolling removes its viewport listener. The separate session harness lets tests unmount the real game and measure that cleanup. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details the active flag, generation checks and scheduling lifetime.

## Keeping a change on the right side

An incorrect pair count starts in the game state and derivation, not in JSX text. An incorrect load-pause state starts in session replacement, not a disabled style. An incorrect arrow stop starts in the numerical navigation helper, while an incorrect scroll alignment starts in the DOM hook. The boundary narrows where an explanation should begin.

The architecture specification permits shared support when two actual behaviors need the same meaning. It does not introduce a generic hooks or utilities layer merely because several files use React. Current direct imports keep ownership legible, and the module policy describes feature placement. Together they make small components useful without making rendering the owner of the game rules.

# CSS organization

This page maps the Neon Pairs stylesheets to their components and explains the global cascade, layout formulas and visual-test seams.

Styles sit beside the behavior they present and are imported by components. They remain ordinary global CSS. File adjacency makes ownership discoverable, while selector choice and the cascade determine actual reach. There is no CSS module transformation, CSS-in-JS runtime or component-library theme layer in this source.

## Stylesheet ownership

| Stylesheet | Importing component or entry | Main responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/game/game.css` | `Game.tsx`; face-sheet entry also imports it | Root theme, page geometry, typography, focus outline and result space |
| `board/board.css` | `Board.tsx` | Viewport scrolling and grid dimensions |
| `board/card.css` | `Card.tsx` | Card states, back, face sizing and matched mark |
| `controls/control.css` | Deal and reproduction components | Shared native-control surface |
| `controls/controls.css` | `Controls.tsx` | Size selector and deal-button arrangement |
| `controls/reproduction.css` | Reproduction components | Disclosure, forms, textarea and load notice |
| `status/status.css` | `GameStatus.tsx` | Statistics and completion presentation |
| `art/face-sheet.css` | Face-sheet entry | Diagnostic placement of real cards |

A component import brings its styles into the application graph, and the build embeds the resulting CSS in the finished HTML. The source HTML has no separate stylesheet link to distribute. [Build pipeline](build-pipeline.md) describes that assembly.

## Global foundation

`game.css` sets `system-ui, sans-serif`, a 16px root font size, 24px line height, light text on a dark background and `color-scheme: dark`. It defines the shared variables `--text`, `--secondary`, `--panel`, `--back`, `--face`, `--border` and `--green`.

The current values are `#f4f6ff` for text, `#b8bdd2` for secondary text, `#141827` for panels, `#1b2034` for card backs, `#111625` for face surfaces, `#757c9a` for borders and `#8bea7d` for matched green. The page background is `#090b14`.

The root also defines `--content-max: 1120px` and `--page-padding: 16px`. A global border-box reset applies to every element, body margin is zero and main uses full width up to that maximum with centered margins and page padding. These foundational rules affect diagnostics that deliberately import `game.css` as well as the main game.

Headings, paragraphs and help text have a small set of explicit margins and font sizes. Secondary text is generally 14px. The global `:focus-visible` outline is 3px white with a 2px offset. Because it is global, its interaction with scroll-container padding matters for cards as well as ordinary controls.

## The board owns its geometry

`board.css` defines board-specific custom properties on `.board-viewport`: card minimum 44px, card maximum 88px, gap 6px, padding 6px and border 1px. The viewport uses `overflow: auto`, contained overscroll, a rounded panel and `max-height: min(70dvh, 768px)`.

The viewport has `width: fit-content` and `max-width: 100%`. The inner board is a grid with a number of columns supplied by `--grid-size`, set from the current game size by `Board.tsx`. Track widths range from the card minimum to maximum.

Its width uses a clamp with these conceptual bounds:

```text
minimum = size * card-min + (size - 1) * gap
preferred = 100% of the available content width
maximum = size * card-max + (size - 1) * gap
```

For size 16, the inner minimum is 794px and maximum is 1498px. The viewport's own padding, border and any scrollbar are separate geometry. A narrow screen can therefore scroll the board rather than shrinking every track without limit or making the whole page wider than the viewport.

The width formula uses the scroll area's content box, which already accounts for occupied scrollbar space. `scrollbars.e2e.test.ts` runs with visible scrollbars at several viewport/size combinations to catch a layout that only works when Chromium hides them.

## Card states come from data

`Card.tsx` supplies `card` plus a state class returned by `describeCard`. `.card` is a square grid-placed native button with full available width, zero padding, a 2px border and an 8px radius. It uses the back surface until revealed or matched, when the face surface applies.

Hover changes the border to the text color. The matched selector appears after the hover selector and gives matched cards the green border. This ordering matters when a matched card remains hovered: its matched treatment continues to win. The class is derived from game data, not a CSS pseudo-state pretending to own the match.

The concealed back is a small rotated bordered span. Visible faces are SVG elements sized to the card. The matched check is a separate absolutely positioned SVG in the top-right corner with width and height at 16% of the card. The source comment explains that a mark much wider than roughly 17% would reach the face's top-right marker.

The card has `scroll-margin: 6px`, which works with nearest scrolling and the global focus outline. Its touch-action and user-selection properties support native pointer behavior. These rules are adjacent to the card because the face sheet also renders the same component outside the normal board layout.

## CSS and SVG share one surface value

The face renderer uses a viewBox of 0 0 100 100. Its main geometry takes the design color, with either a solid fill or outline stroke. A marker circle uses the same color, and its surround stroke is `var(--face)`.

That variable ties SVG geometry to the card's face background. Replacing the card surface without considering the marker surround could make the marker appear to have a mismatched halo. This is a direct dependency between the stylesheet and the inline SVG, even though face identity remains a data mapping in `face-design.ts`.

The matched mark is decorative and uses currentColor from CSS. It is separate from the identity marker, so its size and placement are checked for overlap at the smallest rendered card. [Card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) and [Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md) cover identity design rather than stylesheet placement.

## Shared controls are deliberately narrow

`control.css` defines `.control`: minimum height 44px, padding 8px 12px, a 1px border, 8px radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. Only button and select controls receive the pointer cursor rule. Inputs and textareas have `min-width: 0` so they can shrink within flex/grid layouts.

This class is applied explicitly to the game's form controls. The card component uses its own class and styling. A broad rule for every button would accidentally affect card rendering and diagnostic comparisons, which is why the current selectors distinguish those surfaces.

`controls.css` uses wrapping flex layout with a 12px gap and 16px bottom margin. The size control aligns label and select with a 12px gap. At widths up to 599px, the size row takes full width with spaced ends, while the direct deal buttons share available space.

These rules handle arrangement without replacing native select and button behavior. The CSS does not define a synthetic menu implementation or a separate touch activation model.

## Reproduction layout

The disclosure panel has 24px top margin, panel background, a 1px border and 12px radius. Its summary has a 44px minimum height and 12px by 16px padding. The open body is a grid with 12px gaps and its own inner padding.

The board-code form is a small grid; `.control-row` is a wrapping flex row with a 12px gap. The code input has a 16ch preferred width and flexible growth. The textarea fills its width and can resize vertically. On narrow screens the row buttons share space.

The load-status row sits outside the details element. It reserves at least 56px, wraps its children and gives the notice paragraph flexible width with `min-width: 0`. The conditional Resume button can therefore remain available even when the disclosure is closed. That structure is defined in JSX; the CSS provides room for the state it renders.

The separate `.game-result` area also reserves 56px and vertically centers its content. These reserved areas reduce layout movement when feedback changes. They do not add game-state transitions or determine which message is shown.

## Statistics and completion

`status.css` lays out the definition list with wrapping flex, a 12px row gap and a 24px column gap. Each statistic group has an 8ch minimum width. `dt` and `dd` are inline; labels use secondary text, and values use tabular numerals with reset margins.

Those `dt` and `dd` selectors are global, not scoped under `.stats`. That is harmless for the current single statistic list but is relevant when reading the cascade. File adjacency should not be mistaken for selector encapsulation.

The completion paragraph has padding, border, radius and bottom margin. The `celebrate` class applies a 600ms one-iteration pulse, whose midpoint changes background and opacity. Victory is still a game-derived paragraph after the pulse. A completed import renders the paragraph without that class because the session's celebration flag is false.

## Existing motion rules

The card transitions only border color for 120ms. A reduced-motion query removes that transition. The status sheet has a reduced-motion query that removes the completion animation. These are two local rules beside the elements they affect.

`motion.e2e.test.ts` reads computed transition properties and animation duration/iteration count, then runs with reduced motion and verifies the removals. This checks the browser result of the cascade rather than merely finding a media query in source. The broader motion rationale belongs to [Motion policy](../visuals/motion-policy.md).

## Visual evidence and diagnostic independence

`style.e2e.test.ts` measures root colors, typography, page padding, content maximum, board gap and card geometry. It also compares all computed styles before and after hover to ensure the observed change stays within border colors and checks that hovering does not alter exported progress.

`spacing.e2e.test.ts` inspects margins, padding and gaps in completed and paused-import states at phone and desktop widths. It excludes native option internals. The source's spacing values therefore have runtime evidence across more than the initial closed-panel view.

`art.e2e.test.ts` compares computed styles for a revealed game card and a face-sheet card after excluding placement-dependent properties. This checks that the card does not secretly rely on control styles loaded only by the game. It also measures actual geometry at the diagnostic card size.

For a CSS regression, the relevant chain is selector, inherited variable, rendered state and containing geometry. [Large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md), [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [Visual review checklist](../visuals/visual-review-checklist.md) cover the user-facing outcomes that this organization supports.

# Rules
The rules specification is a game contract that defines turns, scores and session changes in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A turn reveals two eligible cards. A match adds one pair, while a miss gives you time to remember the faces before both cards turn back.

## Board

- R01 - Support square boards with side lengths `4`, `6`, `8`, `10`, `12`, `14` and `16`. Every face occurs exactly twice. Positions run from zero in row order.

The deal comes from the board code defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md).

## Turn

- R02 - The first valid card activation reveals that card. Activating it again or activating a matched card has no game effect.
- R03 - The next valid activation reveals a different unmatched card. If the two faces match, keep them revealed and add one matched pair immediately.
- R04 - If the faces differ, show both for `800` active milliseconds, then close both together. Ignore all card activation during this interval. Pause the interval while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume.
- R05 - Add one move when the second valid card is revealed. The first reveal and ignored activation add no moves. Matches and misses each cost one move until the count reaches `999999`. At that cap the count stops increasing. Play continues normally, pairs still match and the game still completes. Show the current move count throughout play as `Moves: N`.

For example, revealing two matching cards produces one move and one matched pair. Revealing the same first card twice still leaves one revealed card and zero moves.

## Completion

- R06 - Give one point per matched pair and no other score. Show matched pairs against the board's total pairs throughout play as `Pairs: M/T`, where `M` is matched pairs and `T` is the total. Complete the game when every pair is matched. Show the final moves and elapsed time with a completion banner. Apply the completion motion defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).


## Clock

- R07 - Start elapsed time on the first valid reveal. Count active milliseconds while the page is shown. Pause while the page is hidden or an imported snapshot awaits Resume. Stop at completion. Rendering frequency doesn't change the elapsed time. Cap elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds. At the cap, play continues normally and the clock shows the capped time.

Show the clock throughout play as `Time: m:ss`. Round elapsed seconds down, pad seconds to two digits and let minutes continue past 59. For example, 3600000ms shows `Time: 60:00`.

The mismatch interval and elapsed clock use the same active time. Showing the page again continues the interval from its remaining time.

## Session

- R08 - Start with `4` rows and `4` columns unless a saved supported size exists. Remember the last chosen size after reload. A page load starts a fresh deal. Loading a valid board code or snapshot also saves its size as the last chosen size. A failed load keeps the saved size unchanged.
- R09 - New Game creates a fresh seed at the current size. Restart keeps the current board code. Choosing a different size creates a fresh seed at that size. Each action clears the selection, matched pairs, moves and elapsed time.
- R10 - When play completes a game, keep its moves if they beat the saved best for that size. Keep these records after reload. An equal or worse result keeps the existing best. Starting or restarting a game keeps these records. Show the current size's best move count throughout play and after completion as `Best: N`. Before that size has a record, show `Best: none`.
- R11 - Invalid board codes and snapshots show an error and keep the current game. Invalid saved preferences are ignored. If storage is unavailable, play continues without saving.
- R12 - Starting, restarting, replacing or leaving a game invalidates its pending timer updates. An update from an earlier game or turn can't change the current game.

For example, restarting during a mismatch produces the original hidden deal with zero moves. The earlier mismatch timer can't close a card revealed in the restarted game.

Control behavior is defined in [Input](../interface/input.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Input
Input is a set of controls that lets you play Neon Pairs with a pointer, touch or keyboard.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can reveal a card with a tap, then move to its partner with the arrow keys. Every activation uses the same game action, so changing input methods keeps the same turn.

## Activation

The card controls follow these rules:

- I01 - Render each card as a native button. A primary click, a completed tap, Enter and Space activate the card through the same action.
- I03 - Keep the browser's normal context menu on right-click or long-press. Opening that menu doesn't activate a card.
- I04 - Hover and pointer cancellation leave the game state unchanged.

The game decides whether an activation changes a card. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for matches, repeated selections, blocked turns and turn timing.

## Keyboard movement

- I05 - Give the board one remembered tab stop. When Tab enters the board, focus that card. Use the first card before any board focus has been remembered.

- I06 - Move focus with these keys. Movement changes focus without activating a card:

| Key | Focus destination |
| --- | --- |
| ArrowLeft | Previous card in the same row |
| ArrowRight | Next card in the same row |
| ArrowUp | Card in the previous row and same column |
| ArrowDown | Card in the next row and same column |

The board handles only these four arrow keys without modifiers, plus Enter and Space. It leaves every other key and modifier combination to the browser and doesn't use them to move focus or activate a card.

- I07 - Stop arrow movement at a board edge. Moving left from the first column keeps focus on the same card.

- I08 - Let native Tab and Shift+Tab leave the board. Moving through the board uses the movement keys instead of adding every card to the page's tab order.

## Focus

The board keeps focus separate from play:

- I09 - Keep matched cards focusable and mark them `aria-disabled="true"`. Their game action follows the matched-card rule in the gameplay document.
- I10 - While a mismatching pair waits to turn back, allow focus movement and block card activation.
- I11 - On initial load, keep the browser's current focus. Loading the game doesn't move focus to the board.
- I12 - After a new deal, Restart or a successful load, reset the board's remembered tab stop to its first card.
- I13 - When a card receives focus, scroll it into view with nearest alignment in the board's scroll area. Give each card a scroll margin of at least 6px, so its complete focus outline stays in view, including mid-board cards.

The session buttons keep their focus as defined in [Controls](controls.md).

## Card names

The button names describe the information available to the player:

- I14 - Name a hidden card by its one-based row, column and closed state. Keep its face SVG and face identifier out of the DOM while it is hidden, including attributes and accessible text.
- I15 - Name a revealed or matched card by its position, face name and state. Use the face names defined in [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md).

For example, the first hidden button is named "Row 1, column 1, closed". Once revealed, its name includes the face, so a player can remember it without seeing the drawing.

## Announcements

- I16 - Use one polite, atomic live region for turn results and completion. Announce each turn result exactly once. A winning turn has one announcement containing both the match and the win. Consecutive identical results each get their own announcement. Focus movement, clock renders and closing a mismatch don't repeat a result.

Use these turn announcements, where `M` is the matched pair count, `N` is moves and `time` uses R07's display format:

| Event | Announcement |
| --- | --- |
| First match | Pair found. 1 pair matched. |
| Later match | Pair found. M pairs matched. |
| Miss | No match. Cards close after a short pause. |
| Final match | Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time. |

Send the load statuses in Controls through this same live region once per load event. Keep the visible status beside the reproduction controls.

For example, moving across three cards leaves the current announcement unchanged. Resolving the next pair announces that turn's result.

## Screen reader

- I17 - Support a complete 4x4 keyboard game with a screen reader. Find Grid size and New Game by name, enter the board, expose closed positions and revealed faces by name and state, announce one result per turn and make the win, final moves and time available. Leave the board with Tab and start another game. Deliver automated accessibility-tree evidence for this journey. Record the browser and tool versions in the project README and say whether a screen reader was used. If one was used, record its name and version. The user confirms spoken output during acceptance. Spoken confirmation isn't the developer's deliverable.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
---

# Controls
Controls is a specification that defines the game options and reproduction tools in Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

You can start another deal, repeat the current one or load saved progress. Each control keeps the same label, so you can find the same action after a game changes.

## Deal controls

The main controls are:

- C01 - Label the native size select "Grid size". Give it options `4x4`, `6x6`, `8x8`, `10x10`, `12x12`, `14x14` and `16x16`, with numeric side length `N` as each value. After a successful board-code or snapshot load, select the loaded board's size.
- C02 - Label the fresh-deal button "New Game". It creates a fresh seed and keeps the current size.
- C03 - Label the repeat-deal button "Restart". It starts the same board code again.

Changing size, starting and restarting follow the session rules in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md).

## Reproduction tools

- C04 - Put reproduction controls inside a native `details` element that starts collapsed. Give its summary the exact text "Reproduce a game".

The controls use the board-code and snapshot formats defined in [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md). A board code starts a deal. A snapshot loads progress on a deal.

## Load a board

- C05 - Label the text input "Board code" and limit it to 32 characters. Show the current board code after a new deal, Restart or a successful load. Keep an edited draft when a card action changes the game.

- C06 - Label its button "Load board". Validate the entered code before replacing the current game with that deal's starting state.

For example, loading `np1-4-1` starts its hidden four-column board. Entering that code alone keeps the current game until you select Load board.

## Snapshot tools

- C07 - Label the textarea "Snapshot JSON" and limit it to 65536 characters. The parser also applies the UTF-8 byte limit in the snapshot format.

- C08 - Label the export button "Export snapshot". Fill the textarea with readable version 1 snapshot JSON that you can select and copy manually. Export leaves the game state and clock unchanged. It requires no Clipboard API.

Export `elapsedMs` and a pending mismatch's `remainingMs` as whole milliseconds. A pending mismatch always exports at least 1ms.

- C09 - Label the import button "Load snapshot". Validate the complete draft before replacing the current game. Load unfinished progress paused and show "Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue." Load completed progress as completed without pausing and show "Loaded completed snapshot."

- C10 - Show a "Resume" button only while an imported unfinished game is paused. Selecting it clears that pause. Unfinished play continues from the loaded state. While paused, block every card activation and allow board focus movement. On Resume, move focus to the board's remembered tab stop before removing the Resume button. A loaded completed game stays completed and shows no Resume button.

- C11 - On invalid input, keep the current game and the entered draft for correction. Show the exact status for that control:

| Control | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Load board | Invalid board code. |
| Load snapshot | Invalid snapshot. |

- C12 - A loaded completed snapshot keeps the win banner static and plays no celebration. Import doesn't write a best score. Resuming an unfinished snapshot and later winning records a local best under R10.

For example, loading a completed game with fewer moves than the saved best shows that game without replacing the saved record.

## Focus

- C13 - Keep focus on the button used for starting, restarting, loading or exporting. These actions don't move focus to the board. Resume follows C10 because its button disappears. The board's remembered tab stop follows the focus rules in [Input](input.md#focus).

## Replay

- C14 - Keep replay in the developer CLI and game core. V1 has no replay controls in the game UI.

Run `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` to read a replay file. On valid input, print only the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exit 0. On invalid input, print nothing to stdout, write a message to stderr and exit nonzero.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).
