# Visuals
Visuals is a design specification that defines the layout, colors and card artwork for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

A card face combines a shape, a marker position and a fill. You can identify a pair from those features even when you can't distinguish its color.

## Layout

- V01 - Use native controls and a CSS Grid board of DOM card buttons with inline SVG artwork. Render the game without canvas. Use no component library.
- V02 - Center the content within a maximum width of 1120px and give it 16px padding. Keep the outer page within the viewport width.
- V03 - Limit the board's scroll area to `70dvh`, capped at 768px tall. Give it 6px padding and allow overflow on both axes inside that area.
- V04 - Make each card square and size it from 44px to 88px according to the available board width. Use a 6px grid gap, a 2px card border and an 8px card radius.
- V05 - Fit the default four-column board within a phone viewport. When a larger board reaches the 44px minimum card size, keep that size and scroll inside the board.

For example, a sixteen-column board needs 794px for its cards and gaps, plus 12px for board padding. On a phone, the board scrolls while the outer page stays within the viewport width.

The 44px minimum is the chosen card target size. It doesn't state that the complete game conforms to an accessibility standard.

## Colors

- V06 - Use these colors for the page and controls:

| Token | Color | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Page | `#090B14` | Page background |
| Panel | `#141827` | Board scroll area, reproduction panel and non-card button, select, input and textarea backgrounds |
| Back | `#1B2034` | Hidden card background |
| Face | `#111625` | Revealed card background |
| Text | `#F4F6FF` | Main text |
| Secondary | `#B8BDD2` | Help text, status labels and optional supporting text |
| Border | `#757C9A` | Neutral borders |
| Focus | `#FFFFFF` | Focus outline |

- V07 - Use this ordered palette for card artwork:

| Index | Name | Color |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Cyan | `#63E7FF` |
| 1 | Magenta | `#FF71D6` |
| 2 | Green | `#8BEA7D` |
| 3 | Yellow | `#FFE082` |
| 4 | Orange | `#FFB064` |
| 5 | Violet | `#B49AFF` |
| 6 | Rose | `#FF8296` |
| 7 | Ice | `#D9F3FF` |

## Type and spacing

- V08 - Use the system sans-serif font stack. Set body text to 16px with a 24px line height, the title to 24px and secondary text to 14px. Secondary text means help text, status labels and optional supporting text.

- V09 - Use spacing values of 4px, 6px, 8px, 12px, 16px, 24px and 32px for positive layout gaps, padding and margins you set. Allow zero resets and automatic centering. Reset browser default margins. Native control internals aren't covered. Card borders, radii, focus outlines, font metrics and SVG coordinates use their own stated values.

## Card faces

- V10 - Generate 128 face identities from integer face IDs `0` through `127`. Calculate each face from these ordered values:

| Part | Calculation | Ordered values |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | `id % 8` | Circle, square, triangle, diamond, star, hexagon, plus, chevron |
| Marker | `floor(id / 8) % 8` | Top, top-right, right, bottom-right, bottom, bottom-left, left, top-left |
| Fill | `floor(id / 64)` | Solid, outline |
| Color | Palette at marker index | The eight palette colors above |

- V11 - Treat shape, marker and fill as the face identity. Color repeats the marker distinction and doesn't create a separate identity.

- V12 - Draw each face in an SVG with `viewBox="0 0 100 100"`. Center the main shape within `x=25..75` and `y=25..75`. Draw the marker above the shape as a circle with radius 5, centered 40 units from `(50, 50)` in its marker direction. Give the marker a 3-unit stroke in the Face background color, so it stays separate from the shape. Normalize diagonal directions, giving offsets of about 28.284 units on each axis. Use a 5-unit stroke for an outlined shape. At 44px, all 128 identities must be distinguishable in a grayscale face sheet, including solid and outlined squares with diagonal markers.

Use the face color for the solid shape's fill, the outlined shape's stroke and the marker's fill. An outlined shape has no fill. The marker keeps its Face-background stroke.

- V13 - Name each face with lowercase palette, fill, shape and marker names in the form "{color} {fill} {shape}, marker {position}". For example, face `0` is "cyan solid circle, marker top". Face `64` is "cyan outline circle, marker top".

## Card states

- V14 - Give every hidden card the same back with a neutral diamond. Hidden cards keep their face artwork out of the DOM, as [Input](../interface/input.md#card-names) requires.
- V15 - Show the face artwork on revealed cards. Keep it shown on matched cards and add a Green palette border and check mark. Keep matched cards at full opacity.
- V16 - Show keyboard focus with a 3px white outline offset by 2px. Hover changes only the border to the Text color. Matched cards keep their Green border when hovered.
- V17 - Use a 120ms border-color transition. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, turn that transition off.

The gameplay document defines when card states change. See [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md) for turn timing and completion.

## Completion

- V18 - Show a win banner when the game finishes. Give it one 600ms pulse, then keep the banner static. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, show the static banner immediately. Use neither flashing nor confetti.

## Large boards

- V19 - At viewport sizes 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS pixels, render all 256 cards of a 16x16 board. Keep the page within the viewport width and keep controls reachable. Keep each card at least 44px square, with scrolling confined to the board when needed. Reach the first and last card by touch scrolling and by keyboard. Scroll focused cards fully into view without clipping their focus outline.

## Browser zoom

- V20 - At a 640x400 CSS-pixel viewport with device scale 2, the equivalent layout of 200% browser zoom from 1280x800, keep controls, status and the win summary readable without overlap. Keep the page within the viewport width. Keep both a 4x4 board and a 16x16 board playable with pointer and keyboard. Allow board scrolling and keep the focused card and its complete focus outline in view. Don't disable pinch zoom.

The complete game pack starts in [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Reproducibility
The reproducibility specification is a set of versioned formats that recreates Neon Pairs deals, progress and actions.

Status: spec version 2.2. Board codes, snapshots and replays keep format version 1.

A board code reproduces the starting cards. A snapshot restores a later position. A replay shows the actions that produced a position, so each format answers a different debugging question.

## Board code

- D01 - Use `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and `seed` is an integer from `1` through `2147483646`. Use decimal digits without leading zeros. The parser accepts exactly this form. Trim surrounding whitespace in the Board code control before parsing.
- D02 - Version `np1` fixes the generation algorithm below. The same code produces the same deck in every supported runtime. Changing generation requires another version. Time, animation and other random draws can't change this deck.

For example, `np1-4-1` describes a 4 by 4 board with generation version 1 and seed 1. It contains no progress.

## Generate

- D03 - Start the Park-Miller generator at `state = seed`. Each draw sets `state = (state * 16807) % 2147483647`. Use exact integer arithmetic. Seed 1 starts with states `16807`, `282475249`, `1622650073`, `984943658` and `1144108930`.
- D04 - Create the deck as `[0, 0, 1, 1, ...]` through face `N * N / 2 - 1`. Shuffle from index `N * N - 1` down to `1`. At index `i`, draw `j` in `0..i` and swap positions `i` and `j`.

For a draw with `b` possible results, set `q = 2147483646` and `limit = floor(q / b) * b`. Advance the generator and set `x = state - 1`. If `x >= limit`, draw again. Otherwise return `x % b`. This rejection step gives every result the same number of generator values.

The resulting deck for `np1-4-1` is `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`.

## Snapshot

- D05 - Encode progress as a JSON object with exactly `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs` and `started`. `version` is `1`. `matched` is an array of matched position indices. Derive the deck, pair count and completion from these fields.

The `selection` object has one of these forms:

| `kind` | Other fields | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `closed` | None | No unmatched card is revealed |
| `one` | `index` | One unmatched card is revealed |
| `mismatch` | `first`, `second`, `remainingMs` | Two different faces await closing |

- D06 - Validate the complete object before replacing the game. Reject unknown keys. Require unique in-range matched indices containing whole face pairs. Selection indices must be in range and unmatched. A mismatch needs distinct indices with different faces and an integer `remainingMs` from `1` through `800`. Completion requires a closed selection.
- D07 - Require boolean `started` and nonnegative safe integers for `moves` and `elapsedMs`. Reject `elapsedMs` above `359999999` and `moves` above `999999`. Apply the move cap to saved best scores too. Require at least one move per matched pair and one further move for a pending mismatch. If `started` is false, require zero moves, zero elapsed time, no matches and a closed selection. A started game with zero moves requires one revealed card. Import of unfinished progress pauses the clock and pending mismatch until Resume. Completed imports stay completed without a pause.

Illustrative snapshot:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","matched":[0,11],"selection":{"kind":"mismatch","first":1,"second":2,"remainingMs":300},"moves":2,"elapsedMs":1500,"started":true}
```

Importing this snapshot shows one matched pair and two different faces. Resume lets those faces close after another `300` active milliseconds.

## Replay

- D08 - Encode a single deal as `{version: 1, boardCode, actions: [{atMs, index}], endMs}`. Require exactly these fields and exactly `atMs` and `index` per action. Indices must be in range. Times are nonnegative safe integers. Action times must be nondecreasing. If actions exist, `endMs` must be at least the final action time. Equal-time actions keep array order.
- D09 - Start from the code's hidden deal. Advance active time to each action's `atMs` before activating its index, then advance to `endMs`. Resolve a mismatch whose interval ends exactly at an action time before that action. Apply the game rules to ignored activation too. Cap replayed elapsed time at `359999999` milliseconds as R07 requires. Action times and `endMs` keep the nonnegative safe integer range in D08.

Illustrative replay:

```json
{"version":1,"boardCode":"np1-4-1","actions":[{"atMs":0,"index":0},{"atMs":0,"index":11}],"endMs":800}
```

This replay ends with one matched pair, one move and `800` elapsed milliseconds. Replay timestamps use a logical timeline. The game's elapsed clock still starts at its first valid activation. Replay omits hidden-page and imported-pause time. A new deal starts another replay.

## Limits

- D10 - Limit snapshot JSON to `65536` UTF-8 bytes. Limit replay JSON to `1048576` UTF-8 bytes and `10000` actions. Reject malformed JSON and unsupported format versions. For snapshots, inconsistent data means a violation of D05, D06 or D07. For replays, it means a violation of D08 or D09. For board codes, validate D01. Validation checks these stated constraints, without requiring a reconstructed history of earlier turns. Invalid board codes and snapshots keep the current browser game. Invalid replay files are rejected by the CLI and game core.

These local formats and saved scores are untrusted input. Validation checks the state rules, not a verified play history. The game has no accounts or trusted leaderboard.

Turn and clock behavior is defined in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md). Return to [Neon Pairs](../README.md) for the full specification.

# Technology
Technology is the build and language specification for Neon Pairs.

Status: spec version 2.2.

The game runs offline from one HTML file. Browser controls and inline SVG provide the board, input and artwork.

## Stack

- T01 - Use React with TypeScript and DOM rendering. Use native buttons, a native select and CSS Grid. Use no component library.

- T02 - Pin these packages and keep the lockfile. The stable versions were checked on 31 October 2026:

| Package | Version | Job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `react`, `react-dom` | `19.3.1` | Browser UI |
| `typescript` | `7.0.2` | Type checking |
| `@types/react`, `@types/react-dom` | `19.3.0` | React types |
| `vite` | `8.3.5` | Build |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `6.1.2` | React build integration |
| `vite-plugin-singlefile` | `2.3.4` | One HTML distribution |
| `vitest` | `5.0.5` | Unit tests |
| `@playwright/test` | `1.64.1` | Browser tests |
| `@types/node` | `24.19.2` | Build and test types |

TypeScript 7 is a stable release, as the [release announcement](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/typescript/announcing-typescript-7-0/) describes. The [React versions page](https://react.dev/versions) lists the stable React release family.

## Language

- T03 - Use Node.js 24.19 or later and npm. Keep browser and Node compiler projects separate. Use ESM, static imports and type-only imports for types.

Use Node `26.12.1`, npm `11.20.0` and Playwright `1.64.1` with Chromium `156.0.8078.4` as the named compatibility combination. Record the locked install, build, unit tests and browser journeys with those exact versions in the project README before calling the combination tested. Other supported versions need their own results.

- T04 - Enable TypeScript strictness, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `verbatimModuleSyntax` and `erasableSyntaxOnly`. Keep type checking separate from bundling. Vite's [TypeScript support](https://vite.dev/guide/features.html#typescript) transpiles code without checking types.

- T05 - Model project data with exact types and validate unknown data where it enters the game. Use narrowing instead of `any`, suppressed diagnostics or unchecked casts. Derive state unions from their named values.

- T06 - Keep behavior and its code, styles and tests together. Aim for 100 lines per TypeScript file and keep authored TypeScript files at or below 200 lines. Split by behavior when a file grows. Use direct imports from the file that defines a behavior.

## Commands

- T07 - Provide these commands:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `npm ci` | Install the locked dependencies |
| `npm run dev` | Serve the game locally |
| `npm run typecheck` | Check every compiler project |
| `npm test` | Run unit tests for the game rules |
| `npm run test:e2e` | Build from current source, then run browser checks in fresh contexts against that build |
| `npm run build` | Type check and emit `dist/index.html` |
| `npm run --silent replay -- PATH` | Read replay JSON with the output and exit behavior in C14 |

The browser command must fail if its build fails. It must never fall back to an earlier `dist`. Stop development servers and watchers you start before finishing the work.

## Distribution

- T08 - `dist/index.html` contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play. It opens directly from disk without another file or a network request. Use the system font. Keep browser zoom enabled.

- T09 - Serve the game from a local HTTP origin when checking saved preferences. Storage on a `file:` URL differs between browsers, as the [localStorage documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/localStorage) explains. If storage is unavailable, play continues for the current session.

- T10 - Keep dependencies in development and build tooling where possible. The game uses no service, account, external asset, analytics or API key. Dependency installation can use the network. Playing the distribution doesn't use it.

The [game specification](../README.md) connects this stack to the other requirements.

# Acceptance
Acceptance is a set of journeys that checks whether Neon Pairs meets its product requirements.

Status: spec version 2.2.

Finish a game, then start another one during a mismatch. The first journey checks play and completion. The second checks that an earlier timer can't change a new game.

## Play

Use these journeys with the requirements in [Rules](../gameplay/rules.md):

- Finish every supported size with complete pairs.
- Reveal one card twice, then reveal a different card. Check the exact move count.
- Match a pair, then miss a pair. Check the immediate match and the 800ms active mismatch interval.
- Hide the page during a mismatch, then return and finish its remaining interval.
- Start and restart during a mismatch. Check the cleared state and later timer updates.
- Finish games with better, equal and worse move counts. Reload and check the current size's best.

## Controls

Use pointer, touch and keyboard to follow [Input](../interface/input.md) and [Controls](../interface/controls.md). Check control labels, row movement, edge stops, native Tab exit and focus after each action. Check that hidden cards reveal no identity in the DOM.

Follow the keyboard journey in I17 and check its accessibility tree. During user acceptance, confirm spoken results with a screen reader, including consecutive identical results and the final match with its win.

## Appearance

Measure the layout and review all 128 faces against [Visuals](../visuals/visuals.md). Use a 44px grayscale face sheet to distinguish shape, marker and fill. Check 16x16 boards at both stated viewport sizes, full focus outlines and the equivalent zoom layout. Check reduced motion and the static completion banner after its single pulse.

Play through completion and reset while checking [Sound](../sound/sound.md). Every action stays silent.

## Reproduction

Check [Reproducibility](../sharing/reproducibility.md) with its example deck and replay. Check snapshot round trips and malformed input. Check the exact mismatch timeout before an equal-time replay action.

Load an unfinished snapshot, attempt input while paused, then Resume. Check its remaining active time and focus. Load a completed snapshot and check its static banner and unchanged best score.

## Delivery

Use a locked install, type check, unit tests and a fresh browser build as defined in [Technology](../architecture/technology.md). Open the resulting HTML directly from disk with network access blocked. Use a local HTTP origin for saved preferences.

Review the pure game functions, browser effects, file sizes and behavior placement against [Architecture](../architecture/architecture.md).

Back to [Neon Pairs](../README.md).

# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.

`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.

The exact grammar is in [board code format](../sharing/board-code-format.md); the fixed generation algorithm is in [deck generation](../gameplay/deck-generation.md). Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.

The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.

## Why a code repeats an arrangement

The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.

The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.

The published example `np1-4-1` produces `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`. In that deck, positions 0 and 11 contain face 6. That gives a reviewer a literal check independent of what a screenshot seems to show.

`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.

That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.

The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. [Snapshot format](../sharing/snapshot-format.md) and [snapshot selection notes](../sharing/snapshot-selection-notes.md) explain those existing fields.

The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

## What reproducibility can establish

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.

During an investigation, a full board code is more precise than “the small board” or a seed copied without its size. A snapshot can add the state at the moment of interest. A replay can add timed actions. None of these existing artifacts carries a competition participant model. Their usefulness comes from the game information they actually encode.

[Sharing FAQ](../sharing/sharing-faq.md) explains the ordinary tools, and [competition research](competition-research.md) explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.

# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ada | 12 | 70200 | Ahead on moves |
| Bo | 13 | 58100 | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cora | 15 | 65200 | Ahead on active time |
| Dev | 15 | 65900 | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. [Competition pairing](competition-pairing.md) supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

[Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md), [clock design](../architecture/clock-design.md) and [mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. [Replay format](../sharing/replay-format.md) explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

# Competition results and local records

This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs.

The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences.

## The competition boundary

A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board.

For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other.

The comparison between participants is in [competition ties](competition-ties.md). Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time.

## What the game saves today

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values.

An example stored value is:

```json
{
  "schemaVersion": 1,
  "size": 10,
  "bestMoves": {
    "4": 12,
    "6": 24
  }
}
```

There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide.

The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history.

[Preferences store](../persistence/preferences-store.md) and [best score records](../gameplay/best-score-records.md) explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format.

## Two ordinary paths have side effects

The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game.

The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object.

Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game.

There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller.

## Where saving actually happens

`useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted.

Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize.

The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload.

`rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. [Persistence overview](../persistence/persistence-overview.md) and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) cover those existing responsibilities.

## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy

The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best.

That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path.

`src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot.

## A concrete review example

Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8.

The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result.

A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen.

The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear.

# Competition rounds

This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play.

A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in [competition pairing](competition-pairing.md), and the dimensions of the playing board are in [competition boards](competition-boards.md).

## Names during play

The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram.

For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule.

The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device.

## Round, match and board are different contexts

A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage.

Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation.

This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects.

## What the current status component knows

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event.

The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept.

Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. [Status bar](../interface/status-bar.md) explains the existing statistics, and [React boundaries](../architecture/react-boundaries.md) explains the surrounding composition.

This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters.

## A generation is not a round counter

The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component.

That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter.

The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage.

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) and [new game and restart](../gameplay/new-game-and-restart.md) cover the underlying behavior.

## How a sequence can be reviewed

A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images.

The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different.

For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation.

Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. [Focus policy](../interface/focus-policy.md) and [dialog policy](../interface/dialog-policy.md) describe the existing interactions.

# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in [competition deals](competition-deals.md).

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quarterfinal | 4 | 16 | 8 |
| Semifinal | 6 | 36 | 18 |
| Final | 8 | 64 | 32 |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to [competition rounds](competition-rounds.md). The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

[Face catalogue](../visuals/face-catalogue.md), [pair identity](../gameplay/pair-identity.md) and [card artwork](../visuals/card-artwork.md) cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See [large board rendering](../visuals/large-board-rendering.md), [layout grid](../visuals/layout-grid.md) and [zoom behaviour](../visuals/zoom-behaviour.md).

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. [Board keyboard navigation](../interface/board-keyboard-navigation.md) covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The important existing distinction is between a size being technically supported and a stage selecting that size. The ordinary `Controls` component renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. It contains no awareness of the stage mapping on this page. A prototype that simply surrounds those controls with competition text has not made that mapping part of its controller.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.

# Session module

This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences.

The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides a controller for components; the clock and storage hooks perform effects. Keeping those roles distinct makes it possible to explain a click as a sequence of ordinary data decisions followed by rendering and persistence.

## The Session value

`Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves.

These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state.

The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model.

## Initialization

`initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences.

The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Active progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot.

`browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called.

## The current ref and React state

`useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`.

This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game.

The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) follows the component consequences.

## Card activation

The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match.

`activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet.

For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn.

A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus.

## Why feedback has an event counter

Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.

A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice.

`loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message.

## Replacing a game

`replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices.

If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation.

A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves.

The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.

## Controller actions

| Controller action | Validation or preparation | Session effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `newGame(size?)` | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game |
| `restart()` | Recreate the current code, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game of that deal |
| `loadBoard(code)` | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice |
| `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice |
| `exportSnapshot()` | Synchronize active clock | Encode latest game and return text |
| `activate(index)` | Synchronize active clock | Apply session activation |
| `resume()` | Reset observation baseline | Clear pause and load feedback |

The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically.

The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact.

## Logical ticks

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too.

A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer.

The hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. [Clock design](clock-design.md) details scheduling, visibility and fractional steps.

## Preferences and effects

`Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`.

`rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect.

`useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails.

The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method.

## Focus is a neighboring concern

The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. [React boundaries](react-boundaries.md) explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session.

## Evidence and investigation

`session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture.

`storage.test.ts` supplies stores that work and stores whose methods throw. Browser environment tests additionally make acquisition of localStorage fail. This separates the browser integration failure from validation and operation failures in the narrow store interface.

For an incorrect result, inspecting `activateCard` establishes the game transition first. If the game is right but the notice, celebration or preference is wrong, `activateSession` and `replaceGame` are the next places to inspect. If the data is right but an interaction sees old values, the controller's synchronization and commit path become relevant. The directory's separation makes those questions answerable without debugging the entire component tree at once.

# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. [Clock design](clock-design.md) discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. [Mismatch interval](../gameplay/mismatch-interval.md) covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. [Elapsed time rules](../gameplay/elapsed-time-rules.md) covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. [Clock design](clock-design.md) follows those cases in detail, and [Test policy](test-policy.md) explains the runners.
